answer.rationale:
memory_c2 is the load-bearing memory here: it is the only record that makes 'switch primary to the low-cost vendor' look safe, and it is exactly the action the 18% mandate and the quote are pulling toward. So it is the one worth spending the single verification pull on. Key questions the archived source should answer: which component and volume class was that switch, was the line running with buffer at the time, what was the qualification lead time, and did the 'quick onboarding / accurate invoicing' claim cover a full demand cycle or just the first few months? Note that memory_c2 speaks to cost and administrative behavior, not to delivery reliability under load — that is a different risk than the one that matters at 94% of committed volume with no buffer and 14 days to expiry. If the source shows a smaller or buffered context, the memory does not transfer.

Intended action absent contrary evidence: negotiate_terms with the incumbent, run tight and guarded. memory_c4 says benchmarking moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms, and memory_c6 says multi-year commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing service scope — combined, those are a plausible path to a large part of the 18% while leaving the physical supply chain untouched, which is the only variable that protects the 94%-utilization line. A cold primary-vendor switch inside 14 days with no buffer converts a cost problem into a delivery-failure problem; qualification and ramp risk is unpriced in memory_c2. memory_c3 (second source) is attractive on resilience but consumes the one decision this cycle without addressing the mandate; it is the natural next-cycle move, and the low-cost vendor is the right candidate to qualify there at small volume rather than as primary.

Downstream risk flagged: the 18% target may not be fully reachable through negotiation alone. If negotiation lands short, the gap should be escalated to finance as a stated shortfall rather than closed by silently accepting delivery risk — a missed delivery commitment at 94% utilization is a larger loss than the residual spend. I am also not treating any of these memories as settled: all six are consolidated summaries with archived sources, they describe different components and different market conditions, and none of them was recorded under a no-buffer constraint. Decision remains reversible pending the archive pull; if memory_c2's source shows a genuinely comparable component, volume, and slack profile, I would move to a phased dual-award rather than a full switch.
